When a ping fails, many people assume the packet never reached the destination. Often it
was dropped because one router on the return trip had no route back to the source network. The error message tells you which half of the trip failed:
An unknown failure. The packet or its reply was lost. Often a missing
route, a down link or a firewall.

Looking up every packet in a table with thousands of routes would use huge amounts of CPU. Cisco uses three forwarding methods:
The CPU looks up every packet in the routing table and finds the exit interface. This is the original method from Cisco's first router in 1990.
Slowest. Used only for special traffic today.

Which routing-protocol class does OSPF belong to, and how does it send updates?
Link state; triggered updates of changes only, plus hello keepalives - RIP, by contrast, sends the whole table every 30 seconds.

Why can two routes to the same destination, one static (AD 1) and one OSPF (AD 110), exist without conflict?
The router installs only the one with the lowest AD, the static route; the OSPF route is not used while the static one exists - that is how floating statics are made to wait: give them a higher AD.
